doc.title: Randy Brecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 12, 2022

title: Clifford Brown's sound and Philly trumpeters
summary: Brown's sound and melodicism moved Brecker and his father; other Philly trumpeters and Brown's straight-living life.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Thank you, you just answered one of my questions in front of me, how you keep inspired. Let me run a couple of names by you and see if you have any recollections. You had mentioned Clifford Brown early on. What was it about him that was so distinctive?

Well as a kid just his sound and the melodicism and the passion and the beautiful sound he got out of the trumpet. It was heartfelt. It made me cry. It made my dad cry when we’d hear him play a ballad. I remember, and I was only — he died when I was ten years old so this was early on I grew up with him, at least the last five or six years of his career when he was in Philly dad had all the records. He’d play a ballad and I remember Dad kind of grabbed me and said, “Randy, trumpet’s the greatest jazz instrument.” And I took that to heart. Because there were also other good trumpet players around Philly although it was more of a tenor player town, but Red Rodney was around, a guy named Burt

Collins, and there were some really good players, and the guy Bobby Mojica was great — he would come over to our house. So I think he was like a friend even though we never met him. I had never heard him play. Dad would go hear him all the time. I wish I could have. I knew his wife very well. After he passed away she was around on the scene quite a bit. But what a sound. I don’t think — there are certain things he did that have never been surpassed, just the melodicism, the beauty of everything he played.
Yeah. The “Clifford Brown with Strings” — when he enters in that first cut it’s like whoa.

Yeah. It just brings tears to your eyes and it’s all in the sound. And he was like that as a man from what I’ve read and a lot of the cats had substance abuse problems and grew up among other musicians who were all geniuses but had personal problems. He was a straight liver — you know he just went his own way and just had terrible luck in life with his automobile accidents. There was one earlier where he had almost died.
